name: Underhook Sweep
description: Master the Underhook Sweep from Butterfly Guard in BJJ. Complete breakdown of setup, hook-elevation mechanics, counters, and defenses to come up on top.
summary: The Underhook Sweep is a butterfly guard reversal where the seated bottom player secures a deep underhook, loads the opponent onto a butterfly hook, and falls to the shoulder to elevate and roll them over, coming up to side control.
overview:
Built on the same inside-hook leverage that defines butterfly guard, the underhook sweep weaponizes a single deep underhook to control the opponent's upper body while a butterfly hook elevates their hip. Rather than relying on raw bilateral elevation like the standard butterfly sweep, this variation isolates and rotates the opponent's torso through the underhook, making it especially reliable against opponents who post their hands in or drive forward to pass. The deep underhook prevents the crossface, locks their shoulder line to yours, and turns their body into a single unit that topples over your falling shoulder.

The sweep functions as a hub for the entire butterfly bottom game. Loading the opponent's weight onto the hook and threatening the reversal forces predictable defensive reactions, and each reaction opens a different attack: a wide far-side base feeds an arm drag to the back, a committed whizzer feeds a back take through the dogfight, and a backward retreat opens leg-entanglement entries. When the sweep is stuffed, the position regresses gracefully — a stalled attempt drops you into half guard bottom, while a strong whizzer-and-drive counter can flatten you into half guard, both of which remain re-attack platforms rather than dead ends.

Mastering this single reversal therefore unlocks a chain-reaction system that keeps the top player perpetually reactive. It teaches the core butterfly principles of inside position, weight-loading the hook before lifting, and using an opponent's defensive commitment against them, all of which transfer across the modern seated-guard system.

conditions: Seated butterfly guard established with at least the sweep-side foot actively hooked inside the opponent's thigh

Upright posture on the underhook-side hip, off the back, to create the angle for elevation
Opponent's weight loaded forward and onto the hooked leg rather than based wide and settled
Head tight to the opponent's chest on the underhook side, preventing the crossface

attacker.name: Underhook Sweep Attacker
attacker.description: How to execute the Underhook Sweep from Butterfly Guard in BJJ. Attacking perspective with setup, hook-elevation steps, and counter responses.
attacker.overview: From butterfly guard bottom, the underhook sweep is the seated player's most controlling reversal because it removes the opponent's upper body from the equation before the elevation even begins. Securing a deep underhook to the far hip glues the opponent's shoulder line to yours so that when you load their weight onto your butterfly hook and fall to your underhook-side shoulder, their entire torso rotates as one unit over the top. Success depends on a strict sequence — underhook depth, an active loaded hook, posture broken to the sweep side, then a simultaneous fall-and-elevate — followed immediately by coming up on top into side control. Executed well it both reverses position and feeds a web of follow-up attacks when the opponent defends.
key_principles: Secure a deep underhook to the far hip or lat before committing - it controls the upper body so the opponent rotates as a single unit
Load the opponent's weight onto your butterfly hook before lifting - you cannot elevate a based, dead-weight opponent
Elevate with the hook by lifting the knee toward the ceiling, not by kicking the foot laterally
Sacrifice your own base by falling to the underhook-side shoulder to generate the toppling rotation
Time the sweep to the opponent's forward weight commitment - when they post in, drive, or attempt to pass
Come up on top immediately - the sweep is incomplete until you have technical-stood-up into side control
Keep your head tight on the underhook side to deny the crossface and to help drive the rotation
setup_requirements: Seated butterfly guard with the sweep-side foot actively hooked inside the opponent's thigh using the instep
Deep underhook secured on the sweep side, hand reaching the opponent's far hip or wrapping their lat and back
Far hand controlling the opponent's wrist, sleeve, or hugging across their back to remove the far-side post
Upright seated posture on the underhook-side hip, off your back, creating the angle needed for elevation
Opponent's weight loaded forward and onto the hooked-side leg rather than based wide and settled
Head positioned tight on the underhook side to block the crossface and stay connected to the opponent

execution_steps.action: Establish deep underhook and far-arm control
execution_steps.description: From seated butterfly guard, drive your inside arm deep under the opponent's armpit on your chosen sweep side until your hand reaches their far hip or lat. With your other hand control their far wrist, sleeve, or hug across their back. Keep your head tight on the underhook side and your posture upright so their shoulder line is welded to yours.

execution_steps.action: Insert and load the butterfly hook
execution_steps.description: Confirm your same-side foot is hooked actively inside the opponent's thigh with your instep, not merely resting. Pull their upper body into you with the underhook to shift their weight forward and onto that hook, loading their mass onto your elevating leg before you commit. Dead weight that is based out cannot be elevated, so you must feel their weight on your instep first.

execution_steps.action: Break their posture and create the angle
execution_steps.description: Off-balance the opponent toward your underhook side by pulling their shoulder across and down while getting onto your underhook-side hip. This kuzushi removes their ability to post on the sweep side and aligns their center of gravity over your loaded hook, setting the platform for the diagonal toppling motion to come.

execution_steps.action: Fall to your shoulder and elevate
execution_steps.description: Commit to the sweep by falling toward your underhook-side shoulder and upper back while simultaneously lifting the opponent's loaded thigh toward the ceiling with your butterfly hook. The fall generates rotation, the hook generates elevation, and the underhook drives their upper body over the top - all three happening as one explosive, coordinated motion.

execution_steps.action: Pull the far side and complete the rotation
execution_steps.description: As you elevate, pull their far arm or wrist across and drive your underhook through to topple them over your shoulder, eliminating their far-side post. Follow their body, keeping the underhook glued, until they roll past their base of support and your hips begin to come over the top of the rotation.

execution_steps.action: Come up on top into side control
execution_steps.description: Do not stay on your back. As they roll, post with your free hand and technical-standup, chasing the underhook into a crossface as you settle chest-to-chest in side control. Spread your base wide and drop your hips heavy against theirs to deny any immediate guard recovery or scramble back to neutral.

common_counters.counter: Opponent posts their far hand and far leg wide, basing away from the sweep direction
common_counters.your_response: Switch direction using their commitment against them: arm drag to the back as their far side is exposed, or fall the opposite way to sweep toward the open side. A base committed to one direction always opens the other.

common_counters.counter: Opponent whizzers (overhooks) your underhook arm and drives forward to flatten you
common_counters.your_response: Do not fight the whizzer; ride it. Extend your legs and come up to the dogfight to take the back, or hit a single-leg or leg-entanglement entry as they drive. If they smash through, retain half guard rather than staying flat.

common_counters.counter: Opponent pushes your head down and backs their hips away to kill the angle
common_counters.your_response: Re-pummel the underhook deeper and follow them up to your knees rather than staying seated. As their hips retreat and their near arm becomes exposed, transition to an arm drag to the back.

common_counters.counter: Opponent kills your butterfly hook by pinching their knee in and pushing the leg down
common_counters.your_response: Re-insert that hook or switch the sweep to your other active hook. If the hook is fully dead, thread the leg to trap half guard and re-fight for the same underhook sweep from there.

common_counters.counter: Opponent stuffs the underhook and drives a crossface to flatten you to your back
common_counters.your_response: Frame on the hip with your bottom hand, shrimp back to your side, and recover half guard or deep half where the underhook remains effective. Reset the angle and re-attack rather than forcing the original line.

common_errors.error: Attempting to lift before loading the opponent's weight onto the hook
common_errors.consequence: You try to elevate dead weight that is based out, the hook stalls, and you expose yourself to the pass
common_errors.correction: Pull with the underhook to shift their weight forward onto the hook first; only elevate once you feel their mass settle on your instep

common_errors.error: Shallow underhook with the hand stopping at the ribs
common_errors.consequence: The opponent's upper body does not rotate with you, they posture out, and the crossface neutralizes your arm
common_errors.correction: Drive the underhook to the far hip or lat so their torso turns as one unit the instant you elevate

common_errors.error: Kicking the hook laterally instead of lifting the knee upward
common_errors.consequence: You shove the opponent sideways without elevating their hips, so they simply step over or post and stabilize
common_errors.correction: Lift the knee toward the ceiling with your instep, raising their hip off the mat rather than pushing them away from you

common_errors.error: Staying flat on your back instead of falling to your shoulder
common_errors.consequence: You generate no rotational power, the opponent settles their weight back down, and they begin passing
common_errors.correction: Commit to falling onto your underhook-side shoulder to create the toppling rotation, then chase the come-up

common_errors.error: Failing to come up on top after the elevation
common_errors.consequence: You tip the opponent over but stay on your back, allowing them to re-base or scramble back on top
common_errors.correction: Post your free hand and technical-standup immediately, chasing the underhook into a side-control crossface

common_errors.consequence: The opponent frees their leg, re-bases, and passes to the top before you complete the reversal
common_errors.correction: Keep the instep actively lifting until you have rotated past their base and your hips are coming over the top

training_progressions.phase: Phase 1: Static Underhook and Hook Loading
training_progressions.focus: Underhook depth, active hook insertion, and shifting weight onto the hook
training_progressions.description: Partner remains stationary while you drill establishing the deep underhook to the far hip, inserting an active butterfly hook, and pulling their weight forward onto that hook. Focus on feeling the load transfer to your instep before any lift. Drill 10-15 repetitions per side, with the partner giving feedback on underhook depth and weight loading.

training_progressions.focus: Kuzushi to the underhook side and lifting the knee in one motion
training_progressions.description: Partner offers light resistance by basing slightly. Practice breaking their posture to the underhook side, falling to your shoulder, and elevating the loaded thigh simultaneously, allowing the sweep to complete. Repeat 10-15 times per side, emphasizing the coordination of fall, hook lift, and underhook drive as a single explosive movement.

training_progressions.focus: Technical standup into side control after the elevation
training_progressions.description: Add the finish to the rep. Drill rolling the partner through, posting your free hand, technical-standing-up, and chasing the underhook into a chest-to-chest crossface side control under light resistance. The objective is to never finish the rep on your back.

training_progressions.focus: Reading whizzer, wide base, and head-push defenses
training_progressions.description: Partner actively defends with the common counters - whizzer and drive, wide far-side base, head push and hip retreat. Practice branching to the appropriate response: arm drag to the back, dogfight back take, or half-guard and deep-half retention. Emphasis on reacting to the defense rather than forcing the original sweep.

training_progressions.focus: Timing the sweep during passing and standing attempts with full resistance
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts to pass your butterfly guard or stand up with full resistance while you hunt underhook sweep opportunities. Focus on recognizing weight-forward windows and chaining the sweep into back takes and arm drags based on their live reactions. Track which defenses cause the most trouble and build specific solutions.

flashcards.question: When is the optimal moment to initiate the butterfly underhook sweep?
flashcards.answer: The optimal window is when the opponent commits their weight forward - driving into you, posting their hands in, or beginning a pass - because their mass is already loaded toward the sweep direction and onto your hook. Sweeping a settled, based-out opponent whose weight is back will fail regardless of technique, since there is nothing loaded on the hook to elevate.

flashcards.question: Why must you load the opponent's weight onto the butterfly hook before lifting?
flashcards.answer: A based, settled opponent is dead weight you cannot elevate; the hook will simply stall under their immovable mass. Pulling with the underhook shifts their center of gravity forward and onto the hook so the lift actually raises their hip. Loading first is the difference between a hook that elevates a hip and one that just presses against a planted leg.

flashcards.question: How deep must the underhook be and why does depth matter for this sweep?
flashcards.answer: The hand should reach the opponent's far hip or lat. At that depth their torso rotates as a single unit when you elevate, so the upper body topples with the hips. A shallow underhook that stops at the ribs lets them posture out, invites the crossface to neutralize your arm, and leaves their upper body free to counter-rotate against the sweep.

flashcards.question: What is the correct direction of force between the hook and your falling body?
flashcards.answer: Lift the knee toward the ceiling with your instep while falling to your underhook-side shoulder. The hook elevates the hip, the fall creates the rotation, and the underhook drives the torso over the top. Kicking the hook sideways or staying flat produces elevation without rotation, which the opponent simply rides out and re-bases against.

flashcards.question: Your opponent whizzers your underhook arm and drives forward - how do you adjust?
flashcards.answer: Do not fight the whizzer; ride it. Extend your legs and come up to the dogfight to take the back, or hit a single-leg or leg-entanglement entry as they drive forward. If they smash all the way through, retain half guard rather than staying flat. The whizzer only kills the original sweep direction; it actually feeds the back take.

flashcards.question: Your opponent posts their far hand and bases wide away from the sweep - what do you do?
flashcards.answer: Their commitment to one side opens the other. Switch to an arm drag to the back, since their far side is now exposed, or fall the opposite direction for a sweep toward the open side. Forcing the original line against a wide base wastes energy; redirecting to the undefended direction turns their defensive post into your opening.

flashcards.question: Why do many butterfly underhook sweeps stall halfway through?
flashcards.answer: Usually the lifter kicks the hook sideways instead of lifting the knee upward, or stays flat instead of falling to the shoulder, so there is elevation without rotation. Either error lets the opponent re-base before they pass the tipping point. The fix is to combine an upward knee lift with a committed fall to the underhook-side shoulder.

flashcards.question: Your opponent pushes your head down to break your posture - how do you preserve the sweep?
flashcards.answer: Re-pummel the underhook deeper and follow them up to your knees rather than collapsing back into your seat. As their hips retreat and their near arm exposes, switch to an arm drag to the back. The head push is meant to flatten you; meeting it by coming up converts a stalled sweep into a back-take opportunity.

flashcards.question: Why is the sweep incomplete the moment the opponent tips over?
flashcards.answer: Tipping the opponent while you remain on your back lets them re-base, frame, or scramble back on top before you secure anything. You must post your free hand, technical-standup, and chase the underhook into a side-control crossface. The reversal only counts once you have settled chest-to-chest on top with your weight controlling their hips.

flashcards.question: How does the underhook sweep create a complete butterfly attack system?
flashcards.answer: Every defense opens a counter: a wide far-side base feeds the arm drag to the back, a committed whizzer feeds the dogfight back take, a head push and hip retreat feed an arm drag as their arm exposes, and a flatten-out is recovered to half or deep half to reset. The single threat forces reactions, and each reaction becomes the entry to a different attack.

flashcards.question: Your opponent kills your butterfly hook by pinching their knee - what is your option?
flashcards.answer: Re-insert that hook by re-angling your hip, or switch the sweep to your other active hook if it is loaded. If the hook is fully dead, thread the leg to trap half guard and re-fight for the same underhook sweep from there. A dead hook on one side does not end the attack; it just relocates where you elevate from.

flashcards.question: Why does head position on the underhook side matter during the sweep?
flashcards.answer: Keeping your head tight on the underhook side blocks the opponent's crossface, keeps your shoulder connected so the underhook can lift, and helps drive the rotation as you fall and elevate. If your head drifts to the wrong side, the opponent can crossface, separate your shoulder from their body, and posture out of the sweep entirely.

attacker.safety_considerations: The butterfly underhook sweep is a low-risk technique involving no joint locks or chokes, but a few precautions apply. Because the finish elevates and rotates your partner over your shoulder, control the speed of the lift so they are not dropped onto their head or neck - guide the landing rather than launching them. When your underhook is whizzered, do not force the arm against the resistance, as this stresses the shoulder joint; branch to a back take or recover position instead. Keep your head out from under your partner's body during the roll-through, and ensure adequate mat space so the reversal does not carry either player off the training area. When drilling with less experienced partners, scale your explosiveness and let them feel the mechanics before adding speed.

defender.name: Underhook Sweep Defender
defender.description: How to defend the Underhook Sweep from Butterfly Guard in BJJ. Recognition cues, underhook denial, whizzer counters, and base management for the top player.
defender.overview: Defending the underhook sweep from butterfly guard top is fundamentally a battle for the upper body and your own weight distribution. The seated attacker wants a deep underhook, your weight loaded forward onto their butterfly hook, and your posture broken to one side; deny any one of those and the elevation collapses. The highest-percentage defense is prevention - winning the underhook or establishing a two-on-one before they reach depth, while keeping your hips back and your base wide so there is no weight on the hook to lift. Once the underhook is established you must react immediately with a whizzer, flatten them with a crossface, and kill the hook by pinching your knee in, all without diving forward into the very momentum the sweep needs. Reading the setup early and refusing to feed the hook turns their best reversal into a stalled, passable scramble.
key_principles: Win the underhook battle first - fight for your own underhook or a two-on-one before the opponent reaches depth
Keep your weight off their butterfly hook by basing wide with your hips back, so there is nothing loaded to elevate
Whizzer an established underhook to neutralize the lift, but flatten laterally rather than diving forward
Maintain a crossface to drive their head away, killing the angle their torso rotation requires
Kill or pin the hook by pinching your knee in or pushing the leg down to remove the elevator
Never reach your far arm behind you to post - keep your arms in front to deny the kimura and the back
recognition_cues: The attacker's inside arm digs deep under your arm and reaches toward your far hip or lat, not just your ribs
The attacker comes off their back onto their underhook-side hip, angling their shoulders toward you
You feel an active butterfly hook lift under your thigh as they pull you forward to load your weight
The attacker's far hand grips your wrist or sleeve, or hugs across your back, to remove your far-side post
Their head drives tight to your chest on the underhook side, blocking your crossface attempts

defensive_options.action: Contest the underhook early - pummel for your own underhook or establish a two-on-one
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately as the attacker reaches under your arm, before they secure depth to your far hip
defensive_options.if_successful: You deny their primary control, flatten them to their back, and begin your passing sequence from a dominant position
defensive_options.risk: If you contest too late after the underhook is already deep, they may secure the angle and load the hook

defensive_options.action: Whizzer the underhook arm and drive a crossface to flatten them, keeping hips back
defensive_options.when_to_use: Once the opponent has secured a deep underhook and you can no longer prevent it
defensive_options.if_successful: You neutralize the lifting power of the underhook, flatten their shoulders, and can begin passing or threaten a kimura
defensive_options.risk: Over-driving the whizzer forward feeds the dogfight back take, so you must flatten laterally rather than diving in

defensive_options.action: Kill the butterfly hook by pinching your knee in or pushing the leg down, hips back
defensive_options.when_to_use: As you feel them trying to load your weight onto the hook before the elevation begins
defensive_options.if_successful: There is no active elevator, the sweep stalls, and you can pressure forward into a passing position
defensive_options.risk: Reaching down for the leg can break your posture and expose your head if you over-commit

defensive_options.action: Keep your weight off the hook and base wide with a tall, hips-back posture
defensive_options.when_to_use: Throughout the exchange, especially the moment you feel them pulling you forward to load
defensive_options.if_successful: They cannot load and elevate, the sweep never gets started, and the position stays neutral or passable
defensive_options.risk: Staying too tall and static invites the arm drag to the back, so combine base with active hand-fighting

favorable_outcomes.how: Whizzer the underhook arm, drive a crossface across their jaw, and flatten their shoulders to the mat while keeping your hips back. Once they are flat, the underhook loses all lifting leverage; settle your weight and begin your half-guard passing sequence.

Kill the active hook by pinching your knee in and keep your base wide with your hips back so the elevation fails. As the sweep stalls and they retain a half-guard leg, consolidate top half guard with a crossface and start working knee-slice or smash pressure.

common_errors.error: Letting the opponent secure a deep underhook unopposed
common_errors.consequence: Their upper-body control becomes the launchpad for sweeps and back takes, and all later defenses become far harder
common_errors.correction: Contest the underhook from the moment you engage - pummel for your own underhook or a two-on-one and drive your shoulder into their chest

common_errors.error: Loading your weight forward onto their butterfly hook
common_errors.consequence: You hand the attacker the exact elevation the sweep needs, making the reversal nearly automatic
common_errors.correction: Keep your weight back and off the hook, basing wide so there is nothing loaded for them to lift

common_errors.error: Posting your far arm back behind you when you feel the tip
common_errors.consequence: The exposed arm becomes an easy kimura target and provides almost no real base to stop the sweep
common_errors.correction: Post forward or wide with your hand near their head, and recover base with your legs rather than reaching backward

common_errors.error: Whizzering but driving forward too aggressively
common_errors.consequence: Your forward momentum feeds the dogfight back take as they come up underneath you
common_errors.correction: Whizzer with your hips back and flatten them laterally; do not dive your weight forward into the whizzer

common_errors.error: Staying tall and static to avoid the sweep
common_errors.consequence: A passive upright posture invites the arm drag to the back even if it stops the elevation
common_errors.correction: Combine a low, based posture with active hand-fighting to deny both the underhook and the arm drag at once

flashcards.question: What is the single most effective early defense to the butterfly underhook sweep?
flashcards.answer: Win the underhook battle before the attacker reaches depth. By pummeling for your own underhook or establishing a two-on-one and keeping your weight off their hook, you deny the upper-body control the sweep is built on. Prevention is far more energy-efficient than countering a fully loaded, angled sweep, and it lets you flatten them rather than react.

flashcards.question: They have a deep underhook and are loading your weight onto their hook - what is your emergency response?
flashcards.answer: Whizzer the underhook arm, drop your weight back off the hook, base wide, and drive a crossface to flatten their shoulders. You must address all three elements at once - the underhook, the loaded hook, and your base - because a whizzer alone while your weight stays on the hook will still result in being elevated or giving up the back.

flashcards.question: Why is committing your weight forward dangerous against this sweep?
flashcards.answer: Forward weight loads their butterfly hook and aligns your center of gravity over the sweep direction, doing roughly half of the attacker's work for them. The underhook then only has to redirect momentum you are already supplying. The correct adjustment is to keep your hips back and base wide, applying any flattening pressure laterally rather than from a forward dive.

flashcards.question: You whizzer and they extend their legs to come up to the dogfight - what happened and how do you respond?
flashcards.answer: You over-drove the whizzer forward, feeding them the momentum to come up underneath you toward your back. Re-square your chest to them, pull your hips back to break their angle, and re-flatten them before they circle behind. The lesson is that a whizzer must be paired with hips-back pressure, never a forward weight commitment.

flashcards.question: What are the earliest cues that a butterfly underhook sweep is being set up?
flashcards.answer: The first cue is their inside arm digging deep toward your far hip rather than stopping at your ribs. The second is them coming off their back onto their underhook-side hip and angling their shoulders at you. The third is an active hook loading your thigh as they pull you forward. Addressing the underhook depth first prevents the other two from developing.

training_progressions.focus: Winning the underhook or two-on-one from butterfly top
training_progressions.description: Partner works to establish the underhook from seated butterfly while you focus exclusively on pummeling for your own underhook or a two-on-one and driving shoulder pressure. No passing yet - purely win the upper-body control battle and keep them from turning onto their hip. Drill 30-second rounds with reset when either player wins the grip.

training_progressions.focus: Keeping weight off the hook, basing wide, and killing the hook
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes an underhook and attempts to load your weight onto the hook. Practice keeping your hips back, basing wide, and killing the hook by pinching your knee in or pushing the leg down. Partner adds moderate resistance and tries to elevate; focus on never feeding weight to the lifting leg. Drill both sides.

training_progressions.focus: Whizzering without over-driving and defending the branches
training_progressions.description: Partner chains the underhook sweep into the arm drag when you stay tall and into the dogfight back take when you over-drive the whizzer. Practice whizzering with hips back, flattening laterally, and recognizing each chain so you can re-square and re-flatten. Use progressive resistance from 50% to full.

training_progressions.focus: Passing the seated butterfly while defending the underhook sweep system
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring from butterfly top with the goal of passing while defending the underhook sweep. Start standing or in combat base against a seated partner; score for passes, partner scores for sweeps or back takes. Develop the ability to keep weight off the hook and stay offensive rather than purely reactive.

variants_and_adaptations.description: The classic single-deep-underhook version: control the opponent's far wrist or hug their back with the free hand, load their weight onto your same-side butterfly hook, then fall to your shoulder and elevate to roll them over and come up to side control.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent is kneeling or in combat base with their weight committed forward and their hands posting in

variants_and_adaptations.description: Instead of controlling the far arm, bring both arms inside for a body-lock-style clamp around the opponent's torso, then elevate with the butterfly hook and drive them over with the double control. The bilateral upper-body control sacrifices the far-arm pull for crushing torso connection.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent stacks or drives in heavy and squares their shoulders, denying you a clean far-arm grip

variants_and_adaptations.description: When the opponent bases their far hand and leg wide to defend the elevation, abandon the lift and convert the same deep underhook into an arm drag, dragging their near arm across and circling to the back through the dogfight.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent posts wide away from the sweep direction or backs their hips out to deny the loaded hook

variants_and_adaptations.description: From butterfly half guard, combine the trapped leg with the underhook so that the half-guard hook and the deep underhook work together. Use the trapped leg to anchor and off-balance while the underhook drives the rotation, blending half-guard and butterfly mechanics.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When one butterfly hook is cleared during a passing attempt and you retain a half-guard leg with the underhook intact

position_integration: The underhook sweep sits at the center of the butterfly guard bottom system, complementing the standard butterfly sweep by adding dedicated upper-body control through a single deep underhook. Where the basic sweep relies primarily on bilateral hook elevation, the underhook variation isolates and rotates the opponent's torso, making it the higher-percentage option against forward-pressuring, hands-in passers. Its real value is connective: the same underhook that powers the sweep also threatens the back, so a wide defensive base feeds an arm drag, a whizzer feeds a dogfight back take, and a retreating opponent opens leg-entanglement entries. When stuffed, the position degrades into half guard or deep half rather than a finished pass, preserving the bottom player's offense. This makes the technique a foundational teaching tool for inside position, weight-loading the hook, and the principle of using an opponent's defensive commitment against them - concepts that transfer across the entire modern seated-guard game.
